paragraphs.heading: Speeding things up
paragraphs.text: Catalysis is the speeding up of a chemical reaction by an added substance called a catalyst. The catalyst is not used up and comes out of the reaction unchanged. It usually reacts with one or more reactants to form intermediates, which then go on to give the final product and give the catalyst back. When the reaction is quick and the catalyst is recycled fast, a very small amount is often enough.

paragraphs.heading: A different route
paragraphs.text: A catalyst works by letting the reaction follow another mechanism, or pathway, which can be much faster than the uncatalyzed one. This pathway has a lower activation energy, so more collisions between molecules have the energy needed to reach the transition state. The uncatalyzed route is still open, so adding a catalyst can only raise the total rate, never lower it. A catalyst may also make a reaction more selective or let it run at a lower temperature.

paragraphs.heading: Equilibrium stays put
paragraphs.text: Catalysts do not change how far a reaction goes: they have no effect on its chemical equilibrium. The ratio of the forward rate to the reverse rate stays the same. The second law of thermodynamics explains why. If a catalyst could shift an equilibrium, adding it would make the system react toward a new balance and give off energy, and removing it would make the system react back and give off energy again.

paragraphs.heading: Kinds of catalysis
paragraphs.text: Catalysis is called homogeneous when the catalyst is spread through the same phase as the reactants, usually a gas or a liquid. It is called heterogeneous when the catalyst is in a different phase. Enzymes and other biological catalysts are often counted as a third group. A nanocatalyst is a catalyst of nanoscale size, used in applied nanoscience.

paragraphs.heading: Fizzing peroxide
paragraphs.text: Hydrogen peroxide breaks down on its own because the products are more stable, but so slowly that its solutions can be sold commercially. Add a catalyst such as manganese dioxide and the breakdown speeds up a lot, which you can see as oxygen bubbles fizzing out. The manganese dioxide is not used up and can be recovered unchanged and reused again and again. In living things, the same reaction is sped up by enzymes, proteins that act as catalysts, such as catalase.

paragraphs.heading: Everywhere in industry
paragraphs.text: Catalysis is nearly everywhere in the chemical industry. By one estimate, 90% of commercially made chemical products involve a catalyst at some stage of manufacture. One key job is dealing with toxic carbon monoxide: catalysts for its hydrogenation help remove it, cut air pollution and turn it into useful materials. The word catalyst comes from a Greek word meaning to loosen or untie, and the chemist Elizabeth Fulhame came up with the concept from her oxidation-reduction experiments.

paragraphs.heading: Measuring a catalyst
paragraphs.text: Catalytic activity has its own SI derived unit, the katal, measured in moles per second. A catalyst's productivity can be given as its turnover number, or TON. Its activity can be given as the turnover frequency, or TOF, which is the TON per unit of time.
